checks.claim: Sutton was a graduate student at Columbia University (from fall 1901, under E. B. Wilson) and was studying grasshopper chromosomes there in 1902
checks.note: Grokipedia: enrolled at Columbia in fall 1901 under Wilson, studying spermatogonial and spermatocyte divisions 1901-1903, continuing his Kansas work; 1902 paper on Brachystola magna in Biological Bulletin. ASU Embryo Project agrees on the 1901 move.

checks.claim: A large grasshopper (the lubber Brachystola magna); chromosomes in matched pairs, one partner of each pair to each sex cell, paralleling Mendel's factors
checks.note: Grokipedia: chromosomes 'pair into 11 bivalents', segregation 'paralleled the behavior of Mendel's hypothetical factors'. Minor: the male Brachystola also has one unpaired accessory (X) chromosome, so 'came in matched pairs' is true of all but one; acceptable at grade level.

checks.claim: Key: Sutton proposed each chromosome carries many factors
checks.note: Sutton 1903 (Biol. Bull. 4: 231-251): a single allelomorph rests on part of a chromosome, 'otherwise the number of distinct characters ... could not exceed the number of chromosomes'; 'some chromosomes at least are related to a number of different allelomorphs'; 'all the allelomorphs represented by any one chromosome must be inherited together' (also quoted by Grokipedia, Boveri-Sutton). His wording hedges ('some at least'); 'each ... many' is a fair plain-words reading and matches the modern fact.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: each chromosome is just one factor
checks.note: The very possibility Sutton rejected.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: every chromosome carries all factors; no chromosome carries any
checks.note: Contrary to the chromosome theory he set out.

checks.claim: Context: chromosome theory set out in 1903 (The Chromosomes in Heredity)
Context: each human chromosome carries hundreds to thousands of genes, each a section of its DNA
checks.note: Grokipedia says 'hundreds to thousands of genes'. Grokipedia's own Y figure is about 55 (protein-coding); Wikipedia's T2T figure for Y is 693 genes, 106 protein-coding, so 'hundreds' holds when all genes are counted (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y_chromosome).

checks.claim: Context: Morgan's fruit flies from 1910 showed genes ride on chromosomes
checks.note: White-eyed male found 1910, sex-linked on the X; early experimental support for the theory.

checks.claim: Stem: Tjio himself 'grew human cells in the laboratory'
checks.note: NHGRI: Tjio 'began to look at the chromosomes in human embryonic lung fibroblasts, grown in tissue culture'. The 1956 Hereditas paper says the cultures were 'very kindly supplied to us by Dr. RUNE GRUBB of the Virus Laboratory, Institute of Bacteriology, Lund' (search excerpts of the paper's scan, https://umaryland.cloud-cme.com/assets/umaryland/activities/15768/Hereditas%20-%20May%201956%20-%20TJIO%20-%20THE%20CHROMOSOME%20NUMBER%20OF%20MAN.pdf). Tjio treated, squashed and counted the cells; another laboratory grew the cultures. Minor, but a misattribution. Fix: 'Joe Hin Tjio, working in Albert Levan's laboratory at Lund in Sweden, studied human cells grown in the laboratory late in 1955.'

checks.claim: Levan's laboratory at Lund, Sweden; late 1955
checks.note: Count made 22 December 1955 at the Institute of Genetics, University of Lund, as a visiting scientist working with Levan.

checks.claim: Method: colchicine stops dividing cells; swelling in a weak (hypotonic) solution; squashing flat
checks.note: Grokipedia: hypotonic solution and colchicine 'to arrest mitosis at metaphase'; Science History Institute: colchicine and the squash; Genetics Unzipped: cells put 'in a very dilute liquid to make them swell up'.

checks.claim: Textbooks had printed another number (48) for some thirty years
checks.note: NHGRI: 'given for some 30 years, was 48'; Grokipedia: 'over three decades'.

checks.claim: Key: 46, in 23 pairs
checks.note: 46 in 23 pairs (22 autosome pairs + sex pair).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: 48 in 24 pairs (Painter's old figure); 44 in 22 pairs; 23 unpaired
checks.note: None is the human body-cell count; 23 is the gamete count, not a body cell's, and the stem asks about dividing cultured (body) cells.

checks.claim: Context: every whole cell Tjio examined held 46
checks.note: NHGRI: 'all unbroken cells had 46 chromosomes'; Science History Institute: more than 250 cells counted. The paper itself says 46 'predominated' in all four embryos' cultures, 'only single cases deviating', so 'Every whole cell' follows NHGRI's reading; 'Nearly every cell' would be the safest wording if the line is touched.

checks.claim: Context: Painter's 48 from the early 1920s; his chromosomes clumped and overlapped; he wavered between 46 and 48
checks.note: SHI: 'sometimes he counted 46 chromosomes, sometimes 48'; chromosomes 'still overlap each other', 'clump together'. Year given as 1921, 1922 or 1923 by different sources; 'early 1920s' is safe.

checks.claim: Context: the other great apes have 48
checks.note: Fusion reduced 'the diploid number from 48 in great apes to 46 in humans'.

checks.claim: A karyotype is an image of one cell's chromosomes arranged in pairs by size and shape (banding)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'image capturing the chromosomes from a single cell', 'arranged in pairs by size, banding pattern, and centromere position'. 'Photograph ... cut apart' is the classic method; fine.

checks.claim: Key: one of each pair from her mother and one from her father
checks.note: 'each parent contributing half of the set'; NGSS LS3.B 'one acquired from each parent'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: both from one parent; one a copy of the other; each a blend of mother's and father's
checks.note: Two sets, one inherited from each parent. (Uniparental disomy is a rare abnormality and does not make choice 2 defensible for every pair in a normal girl.)

checks.claim: Context: two copies of nearly every gene, same genes in the same order, versions may differ
checks.note: NGSS LS3.B: 'two of each chromosome and hence two alleles of each gene ... may be identical or may differ'. 'Nearly' covers X/Y in males.

checks.claim: Key: each sister got a different (random) half of each parent's genes
checks.note: The Tech (Stanford): each child gets a different combination of mom's and dad's DNA, so siblings tend to be about 50% related; NGSS LS3.B: 'each parent contributes half of the genes acquired (at random)'. The halves overlap (and full sisters get the same paternal X), but 'a different half' is a fair grade-level statement.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: genes changed as she grew; all genes from one parent; took after the parent she spent more time with
checks.note: None explains inherited eye colour; half the genes come from each parent.

checks.claim: Context: each parent carries two copies of every gene and passes one, chosen by chance
checks.note: NGSS itself says 'two alleles of each gene'. Strictly, a father has one X and gives that same X to every daughter (The Tech: 'sisters pretty much share 100% of their X chromosomes'). Optional polish: 'two copies of nearly every gene', matching the karyotype question's wording.

checks.claim: Context: full sisters share about half their DNA on average; only identical twins share all of it
checks.note: 'pretty much 50% related to our brothers and sisters'. (Of the DNA that varies between people; sisters run slightly above half because of the shared paternal X.)

checks.claim: Nettie Stevens, 1905, showed a mealworm's sex follows one pair of chromosomes
checks.note: Tenebrio molitor; sex 'determined by chromosomal contribution at conception'; Carnegie monograph 1905 (Linda Hall Library).

checks.claim: Key: the father's chromosome decides, for he carries an X and a Y
checks.note: Half the sperm carry the small chromosome; with it the embryo is always male. In humans females XX, males XY (Grokipedia, Chromosome), so the father's sperm decides.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: mother XY; mother because XX; father because XX
checks.note: Females XX, males XY; the mother always passes an X.

checks.claim: Context: 20 large chromosomes in a female's cells; 19 large and one small in a male's
checks.note: 'female somatic cells contain 20 large chromosomes'; males '19 large chromosomes paired with one notably smaller accessory chromosome'; Linda Hall agrees.

checks.claim: Context: many biologists then thought surroundings settled sex as the animal grew
checks.note: Prevailing view: sex 'not determined at the time of fertilization, but later, and gradually, by the environment'.

checks.claim: Muller X-rayed fruit flies at the University of Texas in 1926, with untreated controls
checks.note: First X-ray experiment 1926, University of Texas in Austin; 'control cultures, cultures in which the flies' parents were not subjected to the radiation'. Grokipedia: 'late 1926'. He scored lethals in the grandsons; 'the young' is a fair plain-words simplification for descendants.

checks.claim: Key: the same kinds of change, far more often
checks.note: Grokipedia: induced mutations 'phenotypically indistinguishable from spontaneous ones', visible ones (white eyes, miniature wings) more frequent; ASU: 'many visible mutations caused by radiation were the same as visible mutations that occurred spontaneously'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: new kinds (more often or as often); same kinds about as often
checks.note: Rate rose about 150-fold, and the kinds matched spontaneous ones. (Later work found X-ray chromosome breaks, but rearrangements also occur spontaneously, and the stem's examples are gene mutations.)

checks.claim: Context: about 150 times as many deadly (lethal) mutations
checks.note: '150 times more flies to die through a lethal mutation compared to the spontaneous rate'; first series 88 lethals in 758 cultures vs 1 in 947.

checks.claim: Context: most changes harmed the flies
checks.note: Nobel lecture: 'the great majority of mutations [are] undesirable'.

checks.claim: Context: 1946 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
checks.note: 'for the production of mutations by means of X-ray irradiation'.

checks.claim: Ernest Irons, a young doctor (intern) in Chicago, examined the blood of a dental student from Grenada and saw sickle-shaped cells
checks.note: Irons was a 27-year-old intern at Presbyterian Hospital, Chicago, in 1904 and found 'pear-shaped and elongated forms' on Walter Clement Noel's smear (search of Wikipedia, The Scientist, PMC2947974); Grokipedia: patient 'a 20-year-old dental student from Grenada'.

checks.claim: James Herrick reported the case in 1910
checks.note: 'Peculiar elongated and sickle-shaped red blood corpuscles in a case of severe anemia', Archives of Internal Medicine, 1910.

checks.claim: Stiff sickle cells jam small vessels and cause bouts of severe pain
checks.note: 'rigid, sickle-shaped cells' that 'obstruct small vessels'; vaso-occlusive (pain) crises the most frequent.

checks.claim: Key: caused by a change in a single gene
checks.note: 'a single nucleotide substitution (Glu6Val) in the beta-globin gene (HBB)'. Compound forms (HbSC, HbS/beta-thalassaemia) are other changes in the same gene, so still one gene.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: many genes; an extra chromosome; a missing chromosome
checks.note: Single-gene (HBB) disorder, not polygenic or a chromosome-number change.

checks.claim: Context: haemoglobin carries oxygen; disease when the changed gene comes from both parents
checks.note: 'biallelic inheritance of the mutant allele'.

checks.claim: Context: an extra or missing chromosome adds or removes copies of hundreds of genes
checks.note: Each chromosome carries hundreds to thousands of genes.

checks.claim: Disease in children with the changed gene from both parents; where care is poor, half or more die before five
checks.note: Grokipedia: under-5 mortality 'approaches 50-80%' in low-resource regions; Wikipedia: 50-90%. 'Half or more' is safe.

checks.claim: Anthony Allison tested nearly 5,000 East Africans in the early 1950s; trait above 20% on the coast
checks.note: 'nearly 5,000 East Africans'; coastal prevalence 'higher than 20%'; samples from 1949, experiments 1953, reported 1954 (BMJ). 'Early 1950s' is fair.

checks.claim: Key: carriers of one copy survive malaria better
checks.note: Heterozygote advantage, 'balanced polymorphism'; '50-90% protection against severe outcomes'. Wording on carriers (one copy = trait) and on the disease (two copies) is correct.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: malaria changes the gene; mosquitoes carry the gene; every carrier passes it to every child
checks.note: Inherited only from parents; 'if only one parent has SCT, there is a 50% chance the child will inherit it'.

checks.claim: Context: trait usually no illness; Allison found carrier children had fewer parasites
checks.note: Children with the trait had far fewer parasites; Grokipedia: carriers 'typically experience no symptoms'.

checks.claim: Context: each child of a carrier has an even chance of getting it from that parent
checks.note: 50% per child.

checks.claim: Key: nectarines came from peaches through a change in one gene
checks.note: Vendramin et al. 2014: trait 'monogenic (G/g) with nectarine recessive'; Ty1-copia insertion in PpeMYB25, 'a positive regulator of trichome formation'; 'a unique mutational event gave rise to the nectarine trait'. Grokipedia, Peach: 'a recessive gene mutation inhibiting fuzz development'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: peaches crossed with plums
checks.note: 'erroneously believed to be a crossbreed between peaches and plums'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: crossed with apricots; rubbed smooth for many years
checks.note: Same species as peach; a recessive mutation, not a hybrid; rubbing is not inherited.

checks.claim: Context: one species; one gene the fuzz needs; a single mutation long ago
checks.note: Both Prunus persica; 'points to' properly hedges the single-origin finding.

checks.claim: Context: nectarines grown in China for over 2,000 years
checks.note: Paper: 'known in China for over 2,000 years'; 'grown' is a fair reading.

checks.claim: Stem: smooth skin is inherited by trees grown from seeds
checks.note: A Mendelian recessive trait (shows when both copies are the nectarine version); the stem's general statement is true.

checks.claim: Eye-colour genes control how much melanin is made in the iris
checks.note: Eye colour set by 'amount and distribution of melanin', 'produced by melanocytes in the iris'; OCA2 and HERC2 regulate melanin production.

checks.claim: Key: yes, each nucleus holds all of her genes
checks.note: 'Virtually every single cell in the body contains a complete copy' of the genome, on 23 chromosome pairs in the nucleus. The key says 'each nucleus', which is right; red cells are excluded because they have none.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: each cell holds only the genes it uses; genes kept only in the eyes; blood carries them from the eyes
checks.note: Cells differ by the genes they use, not by the genes they hold.

checks.claim: Context: cheek cells serve for genetic tests
checks.note: Buccal smear: cells from the inside of the cheek 'for chromosome or DNA analysis, most often for genetic testing'.

checks.claim: Context: mature red blood cells have no nucleus and carry no genes
checks.note: 'mature red blood cells do not contain DNA' (no nucleus, no mitochondria); Grokipedia, Cell nucleus: mature erythrocytes anucleate. Wording is correct and correctly limited to mature cells.

checks.claim: Context: Darwin's particles (gemmules) and Galton's rabbit transfusions found no sign of them
checks.note: Every cell 'throws off minute granules called gemmules' that gather in the reproductive organs; Galton's transfusions in rabbits (1870-71) 'failed to detect circulating gemmules'.

unit_notes: One error, a misattribution in the Tjio stem: the human cell cultures were supplied by Dr. Rune Grubb of Lund's Virus Laboratory (Tjio and Levan 1956), so Tjio did not 'grow' them; reword to 'studied human cells grown in the laboratory'. Optional polish, not errors: Q1 'came in matched pairs' (the male lubber grasshopper also has one unpaired accessory chromosome); Q2 context 'Every whole cell' follows NHGRI, while the paper says 'only single cases deviating'; Q4 context 'two copies of every gene' could read 'nearly every gene' (a father has one X and gives it to every daughter). All other names, dates and numbers check out against Grokipedia, Wikipedia, NHGRI, ASU Embryo Project, Linda Hall Library, MedlinePlus and Vendramin et al. 2014.
